l: I like to see it lap the miles,
And stop to feed itself at tanks;
In shanties by the sides of roads;
To fit its sides, and crawl between,
12242.136.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The show is not the show,
12242.137.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The mountain at a given distance
Approached, the amber flits a little, --
12242.138.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.139.t: A thought went up my mind to-day
l: A thought went up my mind to-day
But did not finish, -- some way back,
I could not fix the year,
Nor where it went, nor why it came
Have I the art to say.
But somewhere in my soul, I know
It just reminded me -- 't was all --
And came my way no more.
12242.139.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: They say that He can heal,
They speak of what we owe;
12242.140.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Though I get home how late, how late!
So I get home, 't will compensate.
That they have done expecting me,
When, night descending, dumb and dark,
To think just how the fire will burn,
Just how long-cheated eyes will turn
To wonder what myself will say,
And what itself will say to me,
12242.141.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.142.t: A poor torn heart, a tattered heart
l: A poor torn heart, a tattered heart,
That sat it down to rest,
Nor noticed that the ebbing day
Nor noticed night did soft descend
Tenderly took it up from toil
Do the blue havens by the hand
12242.142.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I should have been too glad, I see,
Too lifted for the scant degree
My little circuit would have shamed
I should have been too saved, I see,
Too rescued; fear too dim to me
That I could spell the prayer
Earth would have been too much, I see,
And heaven not enough for me;
I should have had the joy
12242.143.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The ocean's heart too smooth, too blue,
12242.144.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And is held low to freezing lips
How sweet it would have tasted,
His table 's spread too high for us
God keeps his oath to sparrows,
12242.145.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: God gave a loaf to every bird,
But just a crumb to me;
I dare not eat it, though I starve, --
To own it, touch it, prove the feat
Too happy in my sparrow chance
It might be famine all around,
I could not miss an ear,
Such plenty smiles upon my board,
I wonder how the rich may feel, --
I deem that I with but a crumb
12242.146.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.147.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: My country need not change her gown,
As when 't was cut at Lexington,
12242.148.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.149.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.150.t: Except the heaven had come so near
l: Except the heaven had come so near,
So seemed to choose my door,
The distance would not haunt me so;
But just to hear the grace depart
Afflicts me with a double loss;
'T is lost, and lost to me.
12242.150.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.151.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I took my power in my hand.
'T was not so much as David had,
But I was twice as bold.
I aimed my pebble, but myself
Was all the one that fell.
Was it Goliath was too large,
12242.152.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.153.t: A shady friend for torrid days
l: A shady friend for torrid days
The vane a little to the east
Who is to blame? The weaver?
12242.153.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Each life converges to some centre
Admitted scarcely to itself, it may be,
Adored with caution, as a brittle heaven,
Were hopeless as the rainbow's raiment
Yet persevered toward, surer for the distance;
Ungained, it may be, by a life's low venture,
12242.154.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Before I got my eye put out,
I liked as well to see
As other creatures that have eyes,
But were it told to me, to-day,
That I might have the sky
For mine, I tell you that my heart
Would split, for size of me.
The meadows mine, the mountains mine, --
As much of noon as I could take
The motions of the dipping birds,
For mine to look at when I liked, --
The news would strike me dead!
So safer, guess, with just my soul
Where other creatures put their eyes,
12242.155.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.156.t: Talk with prudence to a beggar
l: Talk with prudence to a beggar
Of your viands and your wines!
12242.156.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: He preached upon "breadth" till it argued him narrow, --
The broad are too broad to define;
And of "truth" until it proclaimed him a liar, --
The truth never flaunted a sign.
Simplicity fled from his counterfeit presence
As gold the pyrites would shun.
What confusion would cover the innocent Jesus
To meet so enabled a man!
12242.157.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.158.t: Good night! which put the candle out?
l: Good night! which put the candle out?
A jealous zephyr, not a doubt.
How long at that celestial wick
It might have been the lighthouse spark
Some sailor, rowing in the dark,
It might have been the waning lamp
That lit the drummer from the camp
12242.158.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.159.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A deed knocks first at thought,
And then it knocks at will.
And will at home and well.
It then goes out an act,
That only to the ear of God
12242.160.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The palate of the hate departs;
Let him be quick, the viand flits,
Anger as soon as fed is dead;
12242.161.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It's past set down before the soul,
12242.162.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: That if the spirit like to hide,
The soul that asked its shelter
12242.163.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.164.t: Undue significance a starving man attaches
l: Undue significance a starving man attaches
Far off; he sighs, and therefore hopeless,
Partaken, it relieves indeed, but proves us
In the receipt. It was the distance
12242.164.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.165.t: Heart not so heavy as mine
l: Heart not so heavy as mine,
It was as if a bobolink,
It was as if a chirping brook
I pray you stroll once more!
12242.165.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.166.t: I many times thought peace had come
l: I many times thought peace had come,
As wrecked men deem they sight the land
And struggle slacker, but to prove,
12242.166.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.167.t: Unto my books so good to turn
l: Unto my books so good to turn
And pain is missed in praise.
I thank these kinsmen of the shelf;
12242.167.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The maimed may pause and breathe,
12242.168.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I had been hungry all the years;
My noon had come, to dine;
I, trembling, drew the table near,
'T was this on tables I had seen,
I looked in windows, for the wealth
I could not hope to own.
I did not know the ample bread,
The birds and I had often shared
The plenty hurt me, 't was so new, --
As berry of a mountain bush
Nor was I hungry; so I found
12242.169.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: By catching at the twigs that grow
12242.170.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.171.t: To learn the transport by the pain
l: To learn the transport by the pain,
As blind men learn the sun;
To stay the homesick, homesick feet
Haunted by native lands, the while,
12242.171.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I years had been from home,
I dared not open, lest a face
My business, -- just a life I left,
The silence like an ocean rolled,
That I could fear a door,
Who danger and the dead had faced,
Lest back the awful door should spring,
And held my ears, and like a thief
12242.172.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: By means of it in God's ear;
12242.173.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: He has hid his rare life
12242.174.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: All day, among the crowded air,
And -- waking long before the dawn --
Such transport breaks upon the town
It is not bird, it has no nest;
Nor band, in brass and scarlet dressed,
It is not hymn from pulpit read, --
The morning stars the treble led
Some say it is the spheres at play!
Some think it service in the place
Where we, with late, celestial face,
12242.175.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Just lost when I was saved!
Just felt the world go by!
Just girt me for the onset with eternity,
I heard recede the disappointed tide!
Therefore, as one returned, I feel,
Odd secrets of the line to tell!
Some pale reporter from the awful doors
Next time, the things to see
12242.176.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Of all the souls that stand create
When sense from spirit files away,
When that which is and that which was
And this brief tragedy of flesh
When figures show their royal front
To all the lists of clay!
12242.177.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.178.t: I have no life but this
l: I have no life but this,
Nor tie to earths to come,
12242.178.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: In little wealths, -- as girls could boast, --
Of mines I little know, myself,
But just the names of gems, --
So much that, did I meet the queen,
But this must be a different wealth,
I 'm sure 't is India all day
To those who look on you
Without a stint, without a blame, --
Might I but be the Jew!
To have a smile for mine each day,
At least, it solaces to know
Although I prove it just in time
It 's far, far treasure to surmise,
That slipped my simple fingers through
While just a girl at school!
12242.179.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The solemn contract of a life
Still fable, in the isles of spice,
Sweet debt of Life, -- each night to owe,
12242.180.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: "GOING to him! Happy letter! Tell him --
Tell him the page I didn't write;
Tell him I only said the syntax,
And left the verb and the pronoun out.
Tell him just how the fingers hurried,
Then how they waded, slow, slow, slow;
And then you wished you had eyes in your pages,
So you could see what moved them so.
"Tell him it wasn't a practised writer,
You guessed, from the way the sentence toiled;
You could hear the bodice tug, behind you,
As if it held but the might of a child;
You almost pitied it, you, it worked so.
Tell him -- No, you may quibble there,
For it would split his heart to know it,
And then you and I were silenter.
"Tell him night finished before we finished,
And the old clock kept neighing 'day!'
And you got sleepy and begged to be ended --
What could it hinder so, to say?
Tell him just how she sealed you, cautious,
But if he ask where you are hid
Gesture, coquette, and shake your head!"
12242.181.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.182.t: The way I read a letter 's this
l: The way I read a letter 's this:
'T is first I lock the door,
And push it with my fingers next,
And then I go the furthest off
Then draw my little letter forth
Then, glancing narrow at the wall,
For firm conviction of a mouse
To -- no one that you know!
And sigh for lack of heaven, -- but not
12242.182.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.183.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The night was wide, and furnished scant
That often as a cloud it met
The wind pursued the little bush,
To feel if blinds be fast,
12242.184.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Did the harebell loose her girdle
Would the bee the harebell hallow
Would the Eden be an Eden,
12242.185.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The lady dare not lift her veil
12242.186.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The rose did caper on her cheek,
Her pretty speech, like drunken men,
Her fingers fumbled at her work, --
What ailed so smart a little maid
Till opposite I spied a cheek
A vest that, like the bodice, danced
Till those two troubled little clocks
12242.187.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.188.t: In lands I never saw, they say
l: In lands I never saw, they say,
Which, sir, are you, and which am I,
12242.188.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.189.t: The moon is distant from the sea
l: The moon is distant from the sea,
She leads him, docile as a boy,
He comes just so far toward the town,
Oh, Signor, thine the amber hand,
12242.189.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.190.t: He put the belt around my life,
l: He put the belt around my life, --
Deliberate, as a duke would do
Yet not too far to come at call,
That make the circuit of the rest,
To lives that stoop to notice mine
12242.190.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I held a jewel in my fingers
The day was warm, and winds were prosy;
I woke and chid my honest fingers, --
12242.191.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.192.t: What if I say I shall not wait?
l: What if I say I shall not wait?
What if I burst the fleshly gate
What if I file this mortal off,
See where it hurt me, -- that 's enough, --
They cannot take us any more, --
Dungeons may call, and guns implore;
As laughter was an hour ago,
Or laces, or a travelling show,
12242.192.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And when the sun goes down
As will suffice to light her lamps;
Her golden finger on her lip,
12242.193.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Will there really be a morning?
Is there such a thing as day?
Could I see it from the mountains
If I were as tall as they?
Has it feathers like a bird?
Is it brought from famous countries
Of which I have never heard?
Oh, some scholar! Oh, some sailor!
Oh, some wise man from the skies!
Please to tell a little pilgrim
Where the place called morning lies!
12242.194.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.195.t: At half-past three a single bird
l: At half-past three a single bird
And place was where the presence was,
12242.195.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The day came slow, till five o'clock,
Like hindered rubies, or the light
The purple could not keep the east,
Like breadths of topaz, packed a night,
The happy winds their timbrels took;
The orchard sparkled like a Jew, --
A guest in this stupendous place,
12242.196.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The sun just touched the morning;
Supposed that he had come to dwell,
And life would be all spring.
12242.197.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.198.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Without design, that I could trace,
Where men made hay, then struggling hard
Till sundown crept, a steady tide,
And men that made the hay,
12242.199.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: You see, God bless his suddenness,
As if for you to choose,
And shouts for joy to nobody
12242.200.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: An altered look about the hills;
A Tyrian light the village fills;
A wider sunrise in the dawn;
A deeper twilight on the lawn;
A print of a vermilion foot;
A purple finger on the slope;
A flippant fly upon the pane;
A spider at his trade again;
An axe shrill singing in the woods;
All this, and more I cannot tell,
A furtive look you know as well,
12242.201.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: "Whose are the little beds," I asked,
Some shook their heads, and others smiled,
"Perhaps they did not hear," I said;
Whose are the beds, the tiny beds
Nearest the door to wake the first,
12242.202.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Belles from some lost summer day,
Paris could not lay the fold
Venice could not show a cheek
Of a tint so lustrous meek.
As of brier and leaf displayed
I had rather wear her grace
I had rather dwell like her
12242.203.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It is not of the bird
12242.204.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: One of the ones that Midas touched,
Who failed to touch us all,
I never thought that Jason sought
But then I am a rural man,
With thoughts that make for peace.
But if there were a Jason,
12242.205.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I dreaded that first robin so,
And I 'm accustomed to him grown, --
I thought if I could only live
Till that first shout got by,
Not all pianos in the woods
I dared not meet the daffodils,
Would pierce me with a fashion
I wished the grass would hurry,
So when 't was time to see,
He 'd be too tall, the tallest one
Could stretch to look at me.
I could not bear the bees should come,
In those dim countries where they go:
What word had they for me?
They 're here, though; not a creature failed,
Each one salutes me as he goes,
12242.206.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And every blossom on the bush
12242.207.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The skies can't keep their secret!
They tell it to the hills --
The hills just tell the orchards --
A bird, by chance, that goes that way
If I should bribe the little bird,
Who knows but she would tell?
I would not, if I could,
Know what the sapphire fellows do,
12242.208.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Brought out their burrs and mosses
12242.209.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Two butterflies went out at noon
Then stepped straight through the firmament
Though never yet, in any port,
If spoken by the distant bird,
12242.210.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.211.t: I started early, took my dog
l: I started early, took my dog,
Came out to look at me,
And frigates in the upper floor
Presuming me to be a mouse
But no man moved me till the tide
And past my apron and my belt,
And made as he would eat me up
And he -- he followed close behind;
Upon my ankle, -- then my shoes
Until we met the solid town,
No man he seemed to know;
And bowing with a mighty look
12242.211.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I pull a flower from the woods, --
Computes the stamens in a breath,
And has her in a class.
What once was heaven, is zenith now.
When time's brief masquerade was done,
What if the poles should frisk about
I hope I 'm ready for the worst,
Perhaps the kingdom of Heaven 's changed!
Won't be new-fashioned when I come,
And laugh at me, and stare!
I hope the father in the skies
12242.212.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: An awful tempest mashed the air,
The clouds were gaunt and few;
A black, as of a spectre's cloak,
Hid heaven and earth from view.
The creatures chuckled on the roofs
And shook their fists and gnashed their teeth.
The morning lit, the birds arose;
Turned slowly to his native coast,
12242.213.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.214.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A bird came down the walk:
He did not know I saw;
He bit an angle-worm in halves
And then he drank a dew
And then hopped sidewise to the wall
They looked like frightened beads, I thought;
Or butterflies, off banks of noon,
12242.215.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A narrow fellow in the grass
You may have met him, -- did you not,
The grass divides as with a comb,
And then it closes at your feet
A floor too cool for corn.
Yet when a child, and barefoot,
I more than once, at morn,
Have passed, I thought, a whip-lash
I know, and they know me;
I feel for them a transport
12242.216.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The mushroom is the elf of plants,
At morning in a truffled hut
Is shorter than a snake's delay,
I feel as if the grass were pleased
12242.217.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: There came a wind like a bugle;
And a green chill upon the heat
We barred the windows and the doors
On a strange mob of panting trees,
And rivers where the houses ran
The bell within the steeple wild
12242.218.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: If ruff it was of dame
12242.219.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.220.t: I know a place where summer strives
l: I know a place where summer strives
She each year leads her daisies back,
But when the south wind stirs the pools
Her heart misgives her for her vow,
12242.220.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.221.t: The one that could repeat the summer day
l: The one that could repeat the summer day
Were greater than itself, though he
And who could reproduce the sun,
The lingering and the stain, I mean --
12242.221.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The wind tapped like a tired man,
No bone had he to bind him,
His speech was like the push
Let go a music, as of tunes
12242.222.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Saves she all of that for sunsets, --
12242.223.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Somewhat of nods, and somewhat of
12242.224.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: How happy is the little stone
That rambles in the road alone,
12242.225.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It sounded as if the streets were running,
And then the streets stood still.
Eclipse was all we could see at the window,
And awe was all we could feel.
By and by the boldest stole out of his covert,
To see if time was there.
Nature was in her beryl apron,
12242.226.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The rat is the concisest tenant.
12242.227.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And the earth, they tell me,
12242.228.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The wind begun to rock the grass
He flung a menace at the earth,
The leaves unhooked themselves from trees
The dust did scoop itself like hands
The wagons quickened on the streets,
The lightning showed a yellow beak,
The birds put up the bars to nests,
There came one drop of giant rain,
And then, as if the hands
That held the dams had parted hold,
12242.229.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.230.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Where ships of purple gently toss
And then -- the wharf is still.
12242.231.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Oh, housewife in the evening west,
Come back, and dust the pond!
You dropped a purple ravelling in,
And now you 've littered all the East
And still she plies her spotted brooms,
Till brooms fade softly into stars --
12242.232.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.233.t: Like mighty footlights burned the red
l: Like mighty footlights burned the red
12242.233.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Bring me the sunset in a cup,
Tell me how far the morning leaps,
Tell me what time the weaver sleeps
Who spun the breadths of blue!
Write me how many notes there be
How many trips the tortoise makes,
How many cups the bee partakes, --
Also, who laid the rainbow's piers,
Also, who leads the docile spheres
Who counts the wampum of the night,
To see that none is due?
Who built this little Alban house
And shut the windows down so close
Who 'll let me out some gala day,
12242.234.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Blazing in gold and quenching in purple,
Leaping like leopards to the sky,
Then at the feet of the old horizon
Laying her spotted face, to die;
Stooping as low as the otter's window,
Touching the roof and tinting the barn,
Kissing her bonnet to the meadow, --
And the juggler of day is gone!
12242.235.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Farther in summer than the birds,
12242.236.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: As guest who would be gone.
Our summer made her light escape
12242.237.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.238.t: It can't be summer, -- that got through
l: It can't be summer, -- that got through;
There 's that long town of white to cross
It can't be dying, -- it's too rouge, --
The dead shall go in white.
So sunset shuts my question down
12242.238.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And then we knelt in prayer.
We trust that she was willing, --
We ask that we may be.
In the name of the bee
12242.239.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It tried to be a rose
And failed, and all the summer laughed.
12242.240.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A little this side of the snow
And that side of the haze.
Still is the bustle in the brook,
Grant me, O Lord, a sunny mind,
12242.241.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It wraps it, rail by rail,
Till it is lost in fleeces;
On stump and stack and stem, --
Acres of seams where harvests were,
Then stills its artisans like ghosts,
12242.242.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A neighbor and a warrior too,
The snow and he are intimate;
When heaven looked upon us all
The pillow of this daring head
12242.243.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.244.t: Let down the bars, O Death!
l: Let down the bars, O Death!
Too near thou art for seeking thee,
12242.244.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Pray do not ask me how, --
And yet it will be done
As sure as flocks go home at night
If you should get there first,
Save just a little place for me
Close to the two I lost!
For you know we do not mind our dress
I 'm glad I don't believe it,
For it would stop my breath,
And I 'd like to look a little more
I am glad they did believe it
I left them in the ground.
12242.245.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.246.t: At least to pray is left, is left.
l: At least to pray is left, is left.
I know not which thy chamber is, --
Thou stirrest earthquake in the South,
Hast thou no arm for me?
12242.246.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Step lightly on this narrow spot!
Is not so ample as the breast
Step lofty; for this name is told
Or flag subsist, or fame export
12242.247.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.248.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.249.t: A death-blow is a life-blow to some
l: A death-blow is a life-blow to some
Who, till they died, did not alive become;
Who, had they lived, had died, but when
12242.249.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: To see that I made no mistake
The date, and manner of the shame;
That "God have mercy" on the soul
That at the last it should not be
Salute and pass without a hint --
12242.250.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.251.t: I have not told my garden yet
l: I have not told my garden yet,
I have not quite the strength now
To break it to the bee.
I will not name it in the street,
For shops would stare, that I,
Should have the face to die.
The hillsides must not know it,
The day that I shall go,
Nor lisp it at the table,
12242.251.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: They dropped like flakes, they dropped like stars,
They perished in the seamless grass, --
No eye could find the place;
But God on his repealless list
12242.252.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.253.t: The only ghost I ever saw
l: The only ghost I ever saw
He wore no sandal on his foot,
And stepped like flakes of snow.
His gait was soundless, like the bird,
And God forbid I look behind
12242.253.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.254.t: Some, too fragile for winter winds
l: Some, too fragile for winter winds,
Tenderly tucking them in from frost
Never the treasures in her nest
Building where schoolboy dare not look
This covert have all the children
Lambs for whom time had not a fold.
12242.254.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.255.t: As by the dead we love to sit
l: As by the dead we love to sit,
As for the lost we grapple,
Though all the rest are here, --
12242.255.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: With "This was last her fingers did,"
And then 't was put among the dust
A book I have, a friend gave,
Had notched the place that pleased him, --
Now, when I read, I read not,
12242.256.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.257.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.258.t: Their height in heaven comforts not
l: Their height in heaven comforts not,
'T was best imperfect, as it was;
That skirts the acres of perhaps,
The wealth I had contented me;
Then I had counted it until
12242.258.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.259.t: There is a shame of nobleness
l: There is a shame of nobleness
A best disgrace a brave man feels,
One more "Ye Blessed" to be told;
12242.259.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Triumph may be of several kinds.
There 's triumph of the finer mind
One eye upon the heaven renounced
12242.260.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.261.t: Pompless no life can pass away
l: Pompless no life can pass away;
To the same pageant wends its way
12242.261.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Now know I they both visited
But did because they died, -- a fact
12242.262.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I had no cause to be awake,
My best was gone to sleep,
And morn a new politeness took,
And failed to wake them up,
And then I looked at them,
It could not hold a sigh, --
'T was Sabbath with the bells divorced,
The only raiment I should need,
12242.263.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The thinking how they walked alive,
At such and such a time.
A prank nobody knew but them,
How warm they were on such a day:
So short way off it seems; and now,
How pleased they were at what you said;
You try to touch the smile,
And dip your fingers in the frost:
When was it, can you tell,
You asked the company to tea,
And chatted close with this grand thing
That makes the quick of woe!
12242.264.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: To that odd fork in Being's road,
12242.265.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: In it wait till judgment break
12242.266.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: On such a night, or such a night,
On such a dawn, or such a dawn,
There was a little figure plump
Busy needles, and spools of thread,
Strange that the feet so precious charged
Should reach so small a goal!
12242.267.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Is not expressed by suns alone,
It is the gift of screws.
Makes summer when the lady lies
12242.268.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.269.t: I lived on dread; to those who know
l: I lived on dread; to those who know
As 't were a spur upon the soul,
A fear will urge it where
To go without the spectre's aid
12242.269.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: If birds should build as early,
'T is sweet to know that stocks will stand
12242.270.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And yet we guessed it not;
When Death lit all the shortness up,
12242.271.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: One need not be a chamber to be haunted,
One need not be a house;
Far safer, of a midnight meeting
Far safer through an Abbey gallop,
Than, moonless, one's own self encounter
12242.272.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: She died, -- this was the way she died;
And when her breath was done,
Her little figure at the gate
Since I could never find her
12242.273.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Wait till the majesty of Death
Might dare to touch it now!
A lord might dare to lift the hat
Since that my Lord, "the Lord of lords"
12242.274.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Went up a year this evening!
Is all the rest I knew!
12242.275.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Met by the gods with banners
There must be guests in Eden;
Far as the east from even,
12242.276.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: No ruddy fires on the hearth,
12242.277.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.278.t: It was not death, for I stood up
l: It was not death, for I stood up,
And all the dead lie down;
It was not night, for all the bells
Put out their tongues, for noon.
It was not frost, for on my flesh
Nor fire, for just my marble feet
And yet it tasted like them all;
As if my life were shaven
And could not breathe without a key;
When everything that ticked has stopped,
Or grisly frosts, first autumn morns,
But most like chaos, -- stopless, cool, --
Or even a report of land
12242.278.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I should not dare to leave my friend,
Because -- because if he should die
While I was gone, and I -- too late --
Should reach the heart that wanted me;
If I should disappoint the eyes
That hunted, hunted so, to see,
And could not bear to shut until
If I should stab the patient faith
So sure I 'd come -- so sure I 'd come,
It listening, listening, went to sleep
My heart would wish it broke before,
Since breaking then, since breaking then,
Were useless as next morning's sun,
12242.279.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Great streets of silence led away
Here was no notice, no dissent,
By clocks 't was morning, and for night
But epoch had no basis here,
12242.280.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.281.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The spangled gowns, a lesser rank
All these did conquer; but the ones
But we stood whispering in the house,
12242.282.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.283.t: I think just how my shape will rise
l: I think just how my shape will rise
Till hair and eyes and timid head
Are out of sight, in heaven.
I think just how my lips will weigh
That you, so late, consider me,
I mind me that of anguish sent,
And why not this, if they?
Till with long fright and longer trust
12242.283.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.284.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.285.t: Lay this laurel on the one
l: Lay this laurel on the one
Him you chasten, that is he!
12242.285.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It's all I have to bring to-day,
This, and my heart, and all the fields,
Be sure you count, should I forget, --
Some one the sum could tell, --
This, and my heart, and all the bees
12242.286.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: 'T is little I could care for pearls
Or gold, who am the Prince of Mines;
A diadem to fit a dome
12242.287.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.288.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.289.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: How luscious lies the pea within
12242.290.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.292.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: To invest existence with a stately air,
12242.293.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It's such a little thing to weep,
So short a thing to sigh;
And yet by trades the size of these
12242.294.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Three times, 't is said, a sinking man
Comes up to face the skies,
Where hope and he part company, --
For he is grasped of God.
Is shunned, we must admit it,
12242.295.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.296.t: How still the bells in steeples stand
l: How still the bells in steeples stand,
They leap upon their silver feet
12242.296.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Those who read the same edition
Could we stand with that old Moses
Scan, like him, the stately landscape
Low amid that glad Belles lettres
12242.297.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.298.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: My life closed twice before its close;
So huge, so hopeless to conceive,
Parting is all we know of heaven,
And all we need of hell.
12242.299.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: We never know how high we are
Till we are called to rise;
And then, if we are true to plan,
Did not ourselves the cubits warp
For fear to be a king.
12242.300.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: While I was fearing it, it came,
But came with less of fear,
Because that fearing it so long
There is a fitting a dismay,
12242.301.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: There is no frigate like a book
Nor any coursers like a page
This traverse may the poorest take
12242.302.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.303.t: Who has not found the heaven below
l: Who has not found the heaven below
God's residence is next to mine,
12242.303.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A face devoid of love or grace,
A face with which a stone
Would feel as thoroughly at ease
12242.304.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I lost it in the sand,
And though the sum was simple,
And pounds were in the land,
Still had it such a value
That when I could not find it
I sat me down to sigh.
Who sang full many a day,
But when the woods were painted
I had a star in heaven;
And when I was not heeding
And though the skies are crowded,
I do not care about it,
Since none of them are mine.
Shall meet the eye of traitor

12242.305.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: From all the jails the boys and girls
They storm the earth and stun the air,
Alas! that frowns could lie in wait
For such a foe as this!
12242.306.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.307.t: Few get enough, -- enough is one
l: Few get enough, -- enough is one;
Have not each one of us the right
12242.307.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.308.t: Upon the gallows hung a wretch
l: Upon the gallows hung a wretch,
To which the law entitled him.
The one who bore him tottered in,
''T was all I had,' she stricken gasped;
12242.308.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I felt a clearing in my mind
As if my brain had split;
I tried to match it, seam by seam,
But could not make them fit.
The thought behind I strove to join
But sequence ravelled out of reach
12242.309.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: If nature will not tell the tale
12242.310.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And if to miss were merry,
And if to mourn were gay,
12242.311.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.312.t: The farthest thunder that I heard
l: The farthest thunder that I heard
And rumbles still, though torrid noons
But I would not exchange the bolt
For all the rest of life.
It founds the homes and decks the days,
The thought is quiet as a flake, --
12242.312.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.313.t: On the bleakness of my lot
l: On the bleakness of my lot
Late, my acre of a rock
Soil of flint if steadfast tilled
Seed of palm by Lybian sun
12242.313.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A door just opened on a street --
An instant's width of warmth disclosed,
The door as sudden shut, and I,
Lost doubly, but by contrast most,
12242.314.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.315.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Fire exists the first in light,
12242.316.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Fate slew him, but he did not drop;
She felled -- he did not fall --
Impaled him on her fiercest stakes --
She stung him, sapped his firm advance,
But, when her worst was done,
12242.317.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Finite to fail, but infinite to venture.
For the one ship that struts the shore
12242.318.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I measure every grief I meet
I wonder if it weighs like mine,
I wonder if they bore it long,
I could not tell the date of mine,
It feels so old a pain.
I wonder if it hurts to live,
And if they have to try,
And whether, could they choose between,
I wonder if when years have piled --
Of early hurt, if such a lapse
Or would they go on aching still
The grieved are many, I am told;
Death is but one and comes but once,
There's grief of want, and grief of cold, --
And though I may not guess the kind
To note the fashions of the cross,
That some are like my own.
12242.319.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.320.t: I have a king who does not speak
l: I have a king who does not speak;
So, wondering, thro' the hours meek
Half glad when it is night and sleep,
If, haply, thro' a dream to peep
And if I do, when morning comes,
It is as if a hundred drums
And shouts fill all my childish sky,
And if I don't, the little Bird
Within the Orchard is not heard,
For my will goes the other way,
12242.320.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: It dropped so low in my regard
I heard it hit the ground,
And go to pieces on the stones
Yet blamed the fate that fractured, less
12242.321.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.322.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Till sudden I perceived it stir, --
12242.323.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.324.t: I worked for chaff, and earning wheat
l: I worked for chaff, and earning wheat
What right had fields to arbitrate
I tasted wheat, -- and hated chaff,
12242.324.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Minor apparatus, hopper of the mill,
12242.325.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.326.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Remembrance has a rear and front, --
Look to it, by its fathoms
12242.327.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: That such was not the posture
That, in so dense a fuzz,
12242.328.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The brain is wider than the sky,
For, put them side by side,
The one the other will include
The brain is deeper than the sea,
For, hold them, blue to blue,
The one the other will absorb,
The brain is just the weight of God,
For, lift them, pound for pound,
And they will differ, if they do,
12242.329.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.330.t: The bone that has no marrow
l: The bone that has no marrow;
It is not fit for table,
12242.330.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The past is such a curious creature,
To look her in the face
12242.331.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Which if they do not fit for earth
12242.332.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: One would as soon assault a plush
12242.333.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Within its hope, though yet ungrasped
12242.334.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: To fail with land in sight,
12242.335.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: You cannot put a fire out;
Can go, itself, without a fan
And put it in a drawer, --
Because the winds would find it out,
12242.336.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.337.t: A modest lot, a fame petite
l: A modest lot, a fame petite,
A brief campaign of sting and sweet
A sailor's business is the shore,
A soldier's -- balls. Who asketh more
12242.337.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I must not put my foot amiss
For fear I spoil my shoe?
For yet to buy another pair
But bliss is sold just once;
12242.338.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I stepped from plank to plank
The stars about my head I felt,
I knew not but the next
This gave me that precarious gait
12242.339.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.340.t: One day is there of the series
l: One day is there of the series
Seems it, to my hooded thinking,
Had there been no sharp subtraction
Not an acre or a caption
Not a mention, whose small pebble
12242.340.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.341.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Proud of my broken heart since thou didst break it,
Proud of the pain I did not feel till thee,
Proud of my night since thou with moons dost slake it,
Not to partake thy passion, my humility.
12242.342.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: My worthiness is all my doubt,
Conform my soul as 't were a church
12242.343.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.344.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: One blessing had I, than the rest
It was the limit of my dream,
I knew no more of want or cold,
For this new value in the soul,
The heaven below the heaven above
Why floods are served to us in bowls, --
12242.345.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.346.t: When roses cease to bloom, dear
l: When roses cease to bloom, dear,
The hand that paused to gather
12242.346.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Summer for thee grant I may be
For thee to bloom, I'll skip the tomb
12242.347.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Split the lark and you'll find the music,
Bulb after bulb, in silver rolled,
Scantily dealt to the summer morning,
Saved for your ear when lutes be old.
Loose the flood, you shall find it patent,
Gush after gush, reserved for you;
Now, do you doubt that your bird was true?
12242.348.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.349.t: To lose thee, sweeter than to gain
l: To lose thee, sweeter than to gain
'T is true the drought is destitute,
But then I had the dew!
The Caspian has its realms of sand,
12242.349.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Then dinna care! Then dinna care!
Could'st credit me? Could'st credit me?
Thou'll wilted be; thou'll wilted be!
12242.350.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.351.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Loving the hand that sent it,
12242.352.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Before they drop full music on;
Your breath has time to straighten,
12242.353.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: You may forget the warmth he gave,
When you have done, pray tell me,
That I my thoughts may dim;
12242.354.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.355.t: Father, I bring thee not myself,
l: Father, I bring thee not myself, --
I bring thee the imperial heart
I had not strength to hold.
The heart I cherished in my own
Yet strangest, heavier since it went,
Is it too large for you?
12242.355.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.356.t: We outgrow love like other things
l: We outgrow love like other things
And put it in the drawer,
Till it an antique fashion shows
12242.356.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.357.t: Not with a club the heart is broken
l: Not with a club the heart is broken,
A whip, so small you could not see it.
Yet that whip's name too noble
12242.357.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: My friend must be a bird,
Barbs has it, like a bee.
12242.358.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.359.t: He touched me, so I live to know
l: He touched me, so I live to know
That such a day, permitted so,
It was a boundless place to me,
And silenced, as the awful sea
And now, I'm different from before,
As if I breathed superior air,
My feet, too, that had wandered so,
12242.359.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Let me not mar that perfect dream
But so adjust my daily night
12242.360.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I live with him, I see his face;
And that by right that he
I live with him, I hear his voice,
Taught me by Time, -- the lower way,
That life like this is endless,
12242.361.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I envy seas whereon he rides,
The wealthy fly upon his pane,
I envy light that wakes him,
To tell him it is noon abroad, --
12242.362.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A solemn thing it was, I said,
And wear, if God should count me fit,
A timid thing to drop a life
Too plummetless that it come back
12242.363.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The lilacs, bending many a year,
The bees will not forget the tune
The rose will redden in the bog,
12242.364.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.365.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Upon the furthest slope we know;
12242.366.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A lady red upon the hill
A lady white within the field
The tidy breezes with their brooms
Sweep vale, and hill, and tree!
The neighbors do not yet suspect!
And yet how still the landscape stands,
12242.367.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: How out of breath you are!
Oh, March, come right upstairs with me,
I have so much to tell!
I got your letter, and the birds';
That you were coming, -- I declare,
You left for me to hue;
You took it all with you.
He stayed away a year, to call
As soon as you have come,
That blame is just as dear as praise
And praise as mere as blame.
12242.368.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: We like March, his shoes are purple,
Makes he mud for dog and peddler,
Knows the adder's tongue his coming,
Stands the sun so close and mighty
News is he of all the others;
12242.369.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Not knowing when the dawn will come
Or has it feathers like a bird,
12242.370.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.371.t: A murmur in the trees to note
l: A murmur in the trees to note,
A star not far enough to seek,
A long, long yellow on the lawn,
Not audible, as ours to us,
A hurrying home of little men
All this, and more, if I should tell,
Of robins in the trundle bed
Whose nightgowns could not hide the wings,
But then I promised ne'er to tell;
How could I break my word?
So go your way and I'll go mine, --
No fear you'll miss the road.
12242.371.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.372.t: Morning is the place for dew
l: Morning is the place for dew,
12242.372.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.373.t: To my quick ear the leaves conferred
l: To my quick ear the leaves conferred;
I could not find a privacy
In cave if I presumed to hide,
12242.373.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A sepal, petal, and a thorn
A flash of dew, a bee or two,
12242.374.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.375.t: High from the earth I heard a bird
l: High from the earth I heard a bird;
And then he spied a breeze,
12242.375.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I take thee by the hand.
12242.376.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The grass does not appear afraid;
Can stand so close and look so bold
At what is dread to me.
The sedge stands next the sea,
Where he is floorless, yet of fear
But nature is a stranger yet;
The ones that cite her most
Have never passed her haunted house,
To pity those that know her not
That those who know her, know her less
12242.377.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.378.t: To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee,
l: To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee, --
12242.378.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.379.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The sun went out to work,
The day went out to play,
But not again that dew was seen
12242.380.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: His head, a cap and frill.
12242.381.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Sweet is the swamp with its secrets,
'T is then we sigh for houses,
And guile is where it goes.
12242.382.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And visit only where I liked,
And flirt all day with buttercups,
Or chase me if I do,
I said, but just to be a bee
And row in nowhere all day long,
12242.383.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The moon was but a chin of gold
And now she turns her perfect face
Her forehead is of amplest blond;
Her eye unto the summer dew
Her lips of amber never part;
But what must be the smile
Upon her friend she could bestow
And what a privilege to be
For certainly her way might pass
The stars the trinkets at her belt,
12242.384.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: The bat is dun with wrinkled wings
And not a song pervades his lips,
12242.385.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: You've seen balloons set, haven't you?
It is as swans discarded you
Their liquid feet go softly out
They spurn the air as 't were too mean
Their ribbons just beyond the eye,
And yet the crowd applauds below;
The gilded creature strains and spins,
The crowd retire with an oath
The dust in streets goes down,
12242.386.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And workmen finished, one by one,
The low grass loaded with the dew,
The twilight stood as strangers do
With hat in hand, polite and new,
To stay as if, or go.
A vastness, as a neighbor, came, --
A wisdom without face or name,
A peace, as hemispheres at home, --
12242.387.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.388.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A sloop of amber slips away
And wrecks in peace a purple tar,
12242.389.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.390.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: How the old mountains drip with sunset,
How the hemlocks are tipped in tinsel
How the old steeples hand the scarlet,
Have I the lip of the flamingo
Then, how the fire ebbs like billows,
How a small dusk crawls on the village
And the odd flambeaux no men carry
Now it is night in nest and kennel,
Just a dome of abyss is nodding
These are the visions baffled Guido;
12242.391.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: They won't frown always, -- some sweet day
They'll recollect how cold I looked,
Then they will hasten to the door
Who cannot thank them, for the ice
12242.401.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: And makes one lift one's hat,

And then, that we have followed them
12242.403.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

Paid all that life had earned
And now, what life or death can do
Whose garden wrestles with the dew,

'T was not thy wont to hinder so, --
'T is noon, my little maid, alas!
The lily waiting to be wed,

That night should be to thee
Instead of morning! Hadst thou broached
Dissuade thee if I could not, sweet,

12242.407.t: Each that we lose takes part of us
l: Each that we lose takes part of us;
Which like the moon, some turbid night,

12242.408.t: Not any higher stands the grave
l: Not any higher stands the grave
Not any nearer for the child
12242.408.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: As far from pity as complaint,
As cool to speech as stone,
As if my trade were bone.
As far from time as history,
As children to the rainbow's scarf,

l: 'T is whiter than an Indian pipe,
No stature has it, like a fog,
Not any voice denotes it here,
A spirit, how doth it accost?
Each one of us shall be;
12242.410.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: She laid her docile crescent down,

The news that she is gone.
So constant to its stolid trust,
It shames the constancy that fled

12242.412.t: Bless God, he went as soldiers
l: Bless God, he went as soldiers,
Grant, God, he charge the bravest
Please God, might I behold him
I should not fear the foe then,
I should not fear the fight.

l: Where every bird is bold to go,

l: The grave my little cottage is,

12242.416.t: This was in the white of the year
l: This was in the white of the year,
Drifts were as difficult then to think
As daisies now to be seen.
Looking back is best that is left,
12242.416.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.420.t: I wish I knew that woman's name
l: I wish I knew that woman's name,
So, when she comes this way,
To hold my life, and hold my ears,
For fear I hear her say
Just when the grave and I
Have sobbed ourselves almost to sleep, --
12242.420.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Bereaved of all, I went abroad,
And when I sought my bed,
The grave it was, reposed upon
I waked, to find it first awake,

To lose it in the sea,
The grave was finished, but the spade

12242.422.t: I felt a funeral in my brain
l: I felt a funeral in my brain,
Kept treading, treading, till it seemed
And when they all were seated,
Kept beating, beating, till I thought
And then I heard them lift a box,
With those same boots of lead, again.
As all the heavens were a bell,
And I and silence some strange race,
12242.422.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.423.t: I meant to find her when I came
l: I meant to find her when I came;

I meant to tell her how I longed
But Death had told her so the first,
To wander now is my abode;
To rest, -- to rest would be
12242.423.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

Where none of us should be,

l: Tie the strings to my life, my Lord,
Then I am ready to go!
Just a look at the horses --
Put me in on the firmest side,
For we must ride to the Judgment,
But never I mind the bridges,
And never I mind the sea;
By my own choice and thee.
Good-by to the life I used to live,
And the world I used to know;
And kiss the hills for me, just once;
Now I am ready to go!
12242.428.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.429.t: The dying need but little, dear,
l: The dying need but little, dear, --
A fan, perhaps, a friend's regret,

l: It wears a sprig upon its breast,
And will not tell its name.
Some touch it and some kiss it,
12242.430.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.431.t: The soul should always stand ajar
l: The soul should always stand ajar,
He will not be obliged to wait,
Depart, before the host has slid
To seek for the accomplished guest, --
12242.431.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.432.t: Three weeks passed since I had seen her,
l: Three weeks passed since I had seen her, --
'T was with text and village singing
Gracious now to me as any,
12242.432.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.433.t: I breathed enough to learn the trick
l: I breathed enough to learn the trick,
I simulate the breath so well,
That one, to be quite sure
The lungs are stirless, must descend
12242.433.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: When men and boys, and larks and June
Go down the fields to hay!
12242.434.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: If tolling bell I ask the cause.
I'm answered in a lonesome tone;
That bells should joyful ring to tell
A soul had gone to heaven,
Would seem to me the proper way
A good news should be given.
12242.435.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.436.t: If I may have it when it's dead
l: If I may have it when it's dead
If just as soon as breath is out
Until they lock it in the grave,
For though they lock thee in the grave,
Think of it, lover! I and thee
Permitted face to face to be;
After a life, a death we'll say, --
For death was that, and this is thee.
12242.436.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.437.t: Before the ice is in the pools
l: Before the ice is in the pools,
What we touch the hems of
That which sings so, speaks so,
Will the frock I wept in
12242.437.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: I heard a fly buzz when I died;
Was like the stillness in the air
The eyes beside had wrung them dry,
For that last onset, when the king
I willed my keepsakes, signed away
And then the windows failed, and then
I could not see to see.
12242.438.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: Will no one guide a little boat
Just as the dusk was brown,
One little boat gave up its strife,
Just as the dawn was red,
One little boat o'erspent with gales

12242.439.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.440.t: There's been a death in the opposite house
l: There's been a death in the opposite house
I know it by the numb look
The neighbors rustle in and out,
A window opens like a pod,
They wonder if It died on that, --
I used to when a boy.
As if the house were his,
And he owned all the mourners now,
And then the milliner, and the man
To take the measure of the house.
Of tassels and of coaches soon;
12242.440.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

12242.441.t: We never know we go, -- when we are going
l: We never know we go, -- when we are going
We jest and shut the door;
Fate following behind us bolts it,
12242.441.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: As if the cloud that instant slit

I thought that storm was brief, --

l: A clock stopped -- not the mantel's;
An awe came on the trinket!
It will not stir for doctors,

l: Yet not in all the nests I meet
Soft fall the sounds of Eden
Oh, what an afternoon for heaven,

l: A toad can die of light!

l: Far from love the Heavenly Father
Oftener by the claw of dragon
12242.448.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: A long, long sleep, a famous sleep
That makes no show for dawn
By stretch of limb or stir of lid, --
Nor once look up for noon?
12242.449.src: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete

l: 'T was just this time last year I died.
I know I heard the corn,
When I was carried by the farms, --
I thought how yellow it would look
And then I wanted to get out,
I thought just how red apples wedged
And carts went stooping round the fields
I wondered which would miss me least,
And if my stocking hung too high,
Would it blur the Christmas glee,
That not a Santa Claus could reach
But this sort grieved myself, and so
I thought how it would be
When just this time, some perfect year,
